Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A gray tabby kitten curled up asleep on a folded yellow knit blanket on a wooden window ledge, against a blue wall beside a sunny window

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

20 stepsCanvas: 16 x 12 inFocal point: The kitten's sleeping face: the closed eyes, pink nose, white muzzle and paws tucked under its chin Light: Daylight comes through the window on the left, lighting the left and top of the kitten, the top of the blanket rolls, and patches of the ledge; shadows fall to the right and underneath.How this lesson was made

What you need

Brushes

  • 3/4 inch flat: Blend the sky through the windowFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • 1 inch flat: Blend the blue wallFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • old stiff brush: Dab the dark leaves outsideOld stiff flat: worn, splayed bristles, for rough texture like grass and foliage
  • 1/2 inch flat: Block in the white window frameFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #8 round: Press in the dark knit loopsRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • #6 round: Paint the white muzzle, chest and pawsRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • #4 round: Paint the pink ears and noseRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 1/4 inch angle: Pull the tabby stripesAngle: flat cut on a slant, for crisp corners and curves
  • small fan brush: Flick in the light furFan: bristles spread like a fan, for grass, fur, and soft blending
  • #1 liner: Line the closed eyes and mouthLiner: long, very thin bristles, for fine lines like twigs and grass

Also

  • A 16 x 12 in canvas, landscape (hang it that way). Using another size? Scale every measurement.
  • A ruler
  • Water jar and paper towel
  • Palette or paper plate for mixing

Before you start

You're about to paint a gray tabby kitten fast asleep on a chunky yellow knit blanket, on a wooden ledge by a sunny window. The heart of it is the sleeping face: closed eyes, a pink nose, a soft muzzle and paws tucked in. Warm window light and cool blue shadow give it a calm, cozy mood.

The light

Daylight comes in through the window and falls on the kitten's head and back, the rolls of the blanket and long slanting patches of the ledge. Everything turned away from the window drops into shadow, which is why so many steps paint the lit parts and the shaded parts separately.

What this painting teaches

  • Building from pieces (steps 5, 6, 10, 13). You make a big shape from simple pieces: a rectangle, an oval or a circle first, then curved pieces added around it. It builds the window frame, the rolled blanket and the curled kitten. Keep the pieces simple and let them meet; only soften the joins where the shape should look smooth.
  • Press and lift (steps 11, 12, 16). Touch down with the tip of a round brush, press so it spreads, then pull and lift so the mark ends in a point. Rows of these teardrops make the blanket's knit loops, and smaller ones fill the kitten's ears. Too much paint or a slow lift gives a blob, so use less paint and lift quickly.
  • Curved strokes (steps 14, 15). Every stroke bends with the shape, running down and around it, and that's what makes the kitten look round. You use it for the dark shading and again for the muzzle, chest and paws. Keep the darker paint on the shadow side and follow the curve every time.

The way there

First you paint the sky through the window and the blue wall, the things farthest away. Then the window gets its leaves, its frame and the frame's shadows. Next comes the wooden ledge, laid in, darkened and lit with patches of sunlight, so the whole room is finished before anything sits in it. The blanket goes on next, flat first, then dark and light knit loops. Last comes the kitten: a flat shape, then shading, its pale patches, pink ears, stripes and fur. The sleeping face is saved for the very end, because that's where the eye lands.

Strokes to try on scrap paper first

Each one's card is open in the step that first uses it.

  • X stroke, first in step 2.
  • Dabbing, first in step 3.
  • Building from pieces, first in step 5.
  • Horizontal strokes, first in step 7.

  • Press and lift, first in step 11. Try a row of them on scrap paper first.
  • Curved strokes, first in step 14.
  • Thick to thin, first in step 17.

Getting started

The other basics are in the steps where they matter.

Before you start

Not checked yet

  • Two water jars: one to rinse the brush, one kept clean for thinning paint. A big clear jar shows when the rinse water is dirty.
  • A rag or paper towel, to wipe the brush between colors.
  • Put out bigger puddles of paint than you think you need. Big puddles stay wet longer than small smears.
  • Lay your colors out the same way every time, so they're easy to find and don't get dragged into each other.

Keep your colors clean

Not checked yet

  • Wipe the brush on a rag between colors.
  • Rinse it fully before going into white.
  • Rinse often. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  • Mix on the palette, not on the canvas. Two or three colors at most: stop when the color is right.

Keep paint from drying on the palette

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic on a brushstroke stays wet for only a few minutes.
  • Mist the palette lightly with a spray bottle now and then. Only lightly: too much water weakens the paint.
  • Cover the paint when you aren't using it.

Paint thickness and how much is on the brush

Not checked yet

  • Each step's Load line says two different things. How thick the paint is, and how much of it is on the brush. Creamy paint can be a full load or a light one.

How thick the paint is

How much is on the brush

How much water

Not checked yet

  • Keep water to about half the mix or less. More than that makes weak, see-through color that can lift when you paint over it.
  • For covering, use the paint thick, with little or no water.
  • After rinsing, wipe the metal part of the brush dry.
If something goes wrong not checked yet

Fixing a mistake

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic is forgiving. Let the area dry, then paint over it and try again.
  • Don't keep working a spot that's half dry. Leave it, work somewhere else, and come back.

The sky and the wall 2 steps

Cover the far background, the sky through the window and the blue wall, with soft blended color.

Where: Inside the outlined area. Its top is at the top edge, and its left side is at the left edge; it's about 1 1/4 in wide and 5 1/2 in tall.

STEP 1 OF 20 · The sky and the wall, 1 of 2

Blend the sky through the window

  • Start: Start at the top left corner of the canvas, in the narrow strip along the left edge that will be the window.
  • Strokes: Brush side to side across the strip with Pale blue, working down. Without rinsing, pick up White and keep going lower, then stroke back up over the join while it's wet.
  • Where the paint sits: Pale blue sits at the top of the strip and fades to White lower down, because the sky looks lighter near the horizon.
  • Leave: Keep everything outside the strip as bare canvas. The wall and window frame come later.
  • Stop when: The strip is a smooth sky that slants down toward the left edge at its bottom. Blue at the top, nearly White below, no hard line between.
Paints for this step2 paints, 2 new

Basics: Making a color lighter or darker

Making a color lighter or darker

Not checked yet

  • To lighten: add the color to the white a little at a time, not white to the color.
  • White also dulls a color. Too much turns it chalky.
  • To darken: add the dark into the lighter mix in small amounts.
  • For the next lighter value of something, start from the mix you already have and add white, so the colors stay related.

Stroke: Side-to-side blend how to do it, not checked yet

Side-to-side blend

Not checked yet

With. wide flat; 3/4 inch wash brush

Load. Creamy paint. An even coat.

Motion. Start with the darkest color and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up the next lighter color and paint below it. Then stroke back up over the join several times.

What it leaves. Smooth bands of color, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.

Then. Stroke back over each join while it's wet.

Blend two colors side to side

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • A hard line where two colors meet. Add more of the lighter color at the join and blend again.
  • Two very different colors won't blend. Mix a bridge color from the two on the palette (pink and yellow make orange) and paint it between them.
  • The brush is overloaded. Wipe it on a rag. Rinse before going into white.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 2 OF 20 · The sky and the wall, 2 of 2

Blend the blue wall

  • Start: Start at the top edge of the canvas, right where the window's sky ends, and work toward the right edge.
  • As in step 1: You used Pale blue for the sky. Here it is the wall's lightest blue near the window, laid with crossing X strokes and a bigger brush instead of side to side.
  • Strokes: Cross short strokes over each other like overlapping X shapes. Go back over the wet paint with longer side-to-side strokes where you want it smoother.
  • Where the paint sits: Use Pale blue near the sky strip and Wall blue farther toward the right edge, so the wall looks lit by the window. Carry it under the sky strip too, down to the ledge line.
  • Leave: Leave the sky strip alone, and keep the bottom band of the canvas bare. Paint straight through where the frame, blanket and kitten will go.
  • Stop when: The wall covers everything from the window's sky to the right edge, down to the ledge line. You can still see soft criss-cross marks.

The window 4 steps

Turn the sky strip into a window, with leaves outside and a solid frame around them.

Where: Inside the outlined area. Its top is at the top edge, and its left side is at the left edge; it's about 1 1/4 in wide and 5 1/2 in tall.

STEP 3 OF 20 · The window, 1 of 4

Dab the dark leaves outside

  • First: Let the sky strip dry first, or the leaves will smear into it.
  • Start: Start near the top of the sky strip and tap a few loose clumps, then move down the strip.
  • Strokes: Tap with the tips of the bristles, wiping most of the Leaf green off first. Tap one spot more where you want a clump more solid.
  • Where the paint sits: Most of it goes in the bottom half of the strip, where the trees are fuller. Keep the clumps loose and soft-edged, since the trees are far away.
  • Leave: Let the sky show between the clumps. Keep off the wall.
  • Stop when: The strip shows soft, broken clumps of leaves from top to bottom, fuller lower down, with sky peeking between them.

Stroke: Dabbing how to do it, not checked yet

Dabbing also called stippling

Not checked yet

With. round (the tip, for small dots); old stiff brush (for rough patches); a sponge, for soft patches

Load. A light load. No water on the brush: a wet one makes blobs.

Motion. Tap with the tip of the brush. The more you tap one spot, the more solid it gets.

What it leaves. Dots or dappled patches that get more solid the more you tap.

Then. Tap a lighter mix on the lit side, leaving the darker taps showing underneath.

Good for. foliage, with an old stiff brush, small dots, with the tip of a round

Tap, don't stroke

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • Blobs instead of dots. The brush is too wet or holds too much paint. Wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel and tap again.
  • A patch went too solid. Tap over it with a lighter or darker mix to break it up.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 4 OF 20 · The window, 2 of 4

Dab the sunlit leaves

  • First: Let the darker leaves from step 3 dry first so the taps stay separate.
  • Start: Start on the top of the highest clump of leaves in the window strip.
  • As in step 3: Same old stiff brush and the same light taps. This time the mix is lighter and only goes where the sun hits each clump, so the darker taps keep showing.
  • Strokes: Tap lightly with the brush tips, a dry brush with just a little Light leaf green on it.
  • Where the paint sits: Put the taps on the tops and upper edges of each clump, where the sun hits them. Make five or so lighter patches down the strip.
  • Leave: Leave the darker leaves showing underneath each sunlit top, and leave the gaps of sky open.
  • Stop when: Each clump has a sunlit, Light leaf green top over its darker underside. The leaves now look round and lit by the sun.

STEP 5 OF 20 · The window, 3 of 4

Block in the white window frame

  • First: Let the leaves and the wall dry first, or the frame will pick up their color.
  • Start: Start with the tall post that closes the window, just where the leaves and sky end and the wall begins.
  • Strokes: Build it from simple rectangles: pull the post down in straight strokes, then lay a crossbar across the glass near the top, then a wide sill under the glass.
  • Where the paint sits: Keep the edges straight, and let the sill slant down toward the left edge.
  • Leave: Leave the sky and leaves showing in the window panes, between the frame's pieces.
  • Stop when: A flat White frame stands around the window: posts, a crossbar and a slanting sill, with no shadows yet.

STEP 6 OF 20 · The window, 4 of 4

Shade the side of the frame

  • First: Let the frame from step 5 dry completely first.
  • Start: Start with the tall face of the frame where it meets the wall.
  • As in step 2: This is the same Wall blue you used on the wall, so the frame's shadowed faces settle into the wall around them.
  • Strokes: Pull straight strokes down the length of that face, then add thin strips along the post's inner face, under the crossbar and along the front of the sill.
  • Where the paint sits: The Wall blue goes on the faces that turn away from the window light, so the frame looks solid instead of flat.
  • Leave: Leave the frame faces that look toward the light bright and unpainted by this step.
  • Stop when: The frame has a dark band where it meets the wall, thin shadow lines under the crossbar and the sill front, and bright faces everywhere else.

The wooden ledge 3 steps

Lay the wooden ledge and give it shadow and sunlight, so the room is finished.

Where: Inside the outlined area, all the way across to the bottom edge. Its top is about 4 1/2 in from the bottom edge.

STEP 7 OF 20 · The wooden ledge, 1 of 3

Lay in the wooden ledge

  • First: Let the wall and frame dry first so the line where they meet the ledge stays clean.
  • Start: Start at the left edge of the canvas, just under the frame's sill, and fill the bottom band.
  • Strokes: Keep the brush level and pull long strokes from left to right across the whole canvas, working down to the bottom edge.
  • Where the paint sits: The Wood brown covers the whole ledge in one even coat. Its top edge follows the bottom of the wall.
  • Leave: Don't touch the wall or the window frame. Paint right through where the blanket will sit.
  • Stop when: The bottom band is a flat warm brown from edge to edge, with no light or shadow yet.

STEP 8 OF 20 · The wooden ledge, 2 of 3

Darken the front of the ledge

  • First: Let the first ledge coat dry so the darker coat sits on top instead of mixing in.
  • Start: Start at the right edge of the canvas, along the back of the ledge where it meets the wall.
  • As in step 7: Same brush and the same long level strokes. This time the paint is darker, and you leave the slanting sunlit patches uncovered instead of filling the whole ledge.
  • Strokes: Pull long level strokes from left to right, and across the bottom of the ledge too.
  • Where the paint sits: Most of it goes in the right half and along the bottom, away from the window. Leave two long slanting bands on the left half uncovered: that's where the sunlight will fall.
  • Leave: Leave those slanting light patches and the thin dark line between them showing as the first warm brown.
  • Stop when: The ledge is deep red-brown on the right and along the bottom, with long slanting lighter patches left near the window.

STEP 9 OF 20 · The wooden ledge, 3 of 3

Dry-brush the sunlit patches on the ledge

  • First: Let the ledge dry completely. Dry brush only works on dry paint.

STEP 11 OF 20 · The yellow blanket, 2 of 3

Press in the dark knit loops

  • First: Let the blanket's yellow coat dry first, or the loops will blur.
  • Start: Start along the rim of the back roll, where the blanket meets the wall, and work your way across.
  • Strokes: Press the tip down, let the belly spread, then lift as you pull, so each mark is a small teardrop. Set them in pairs leaning together like little Vs.
  • Where the paint sits: Lay rows of loops along each rolled band, darker in the groove between the two rolls and along the bottom, where the light doesn't reach. Scatter looser loops over the flat top.
  • Leave: Leave plenty of plain yellow showing between the loops.
  • Stop when: The blanket reads as chunky knit: rows of darker V loops along the rolls, a dark groove between them and shadow along the bottom.

Pull the tabby stripes

STEP 19 OF 20 · The sleeping face, 1 of 2

Stroke: Liner work how to do it, not checked yet

Liner work

Not checked yet

With. liner; small round (the tip)

Load. Thin paint. Swirl the brush in water, then in the paint. Add water if the line skips. Reload often.

Motion. Hold the brush upright, with light, steady pressure. For a tapering line, start thick and lighten as you go. Let lines fork in different directions and overlap, and wobble the edges a little.

What it leaves. Thin, flowing lines.

Then. Reload often.

Good for. branches and twigs, thick at the trunk and tapering, fine lines and details

Thin paint, upright brush

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • Skippy, broken lines. The paint is too thick. Add water.
  • Lines spread or feather. The paint underneath is still wet. Only paint lines over dry paint.

Try a few lines on scrap paper first.

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: A grey tabby cat curled up asleep on a folded mustard-yellow knit blanket, on a wooden sill beside a window, against a pale blue-grey wall. The source is already a painterly AI-made image.

Found in the image: just the picture

Done: none

Why: No bars, borders, captions, watermark or surrounding scene: the whole image is the scene to paint.

Fitted to your canvas

Canvas: 16 x 12 in, landscape (the default: the standard size closest to the photo's 3:2 shape)

Done: extend

Left out: nothing; about 5/8 in was added at the top (more blue-grey wall) and at the bottom (more wooden sill)

Why: A 4:3 crop of the 3:2 photo would have cut into the cat, whose ear and curled back reach almost to both side edges, so the picture fills the canvas's width and the wall above and the sill below were painted on by one extend render.

Beginner version

What made it too busy: Tiny separate things: no (the garden through the window is a few soft green patches, and the window frame is a few big bars). Hundreds of items: no; the knit blanket's stitches are one repeated mark (short slanted yellow dabs in rows) and busy measured 0.0 fine texture. Detail inside big shapes: no; the tabby stripes are one repeated dark stroke over the grey, and the whiskers are a few liner lines. Parts: about seven (garden view, window frame, wall, sill, blanket, cat, white fur and face), within max_parts 8.

Why: The source is already a loose, simple painting a beginner could copy, with fine texture at 0.0, so a beginner version would only cost money and change nothing.

Fine texture measured: the photo 0.0% of the canvas

A soft, simple scene: a gray tabby kitten asleep on a chunky yellow knit blanket on a wooden ledge by a sunny window. What matters is the sleeping face and the round, furry curl of the body; what's hard is drawing the curled cat and keeping the knit and fur loose. The lesson is about building the room back to front and then the kitten from simple shapes.

Subject: A gray tabby kitten curled up asleep on a folded yellow knit blanket on a wooden window ledge, against a blue wall beside a sunny window
Focal point: The kitten's sleeping face: the closed eyes, pink nose, white muzzle and paws tucked under its chin
Light: Daylight comes through the window on the left, lighting the left and top of the kitten, the top of the blanket rolls, and patches of the ledge; shadows fall to the right and underneath.

What it saw, back to front

  1. The pale sky through the window
  2. The blue wall
  3. The white window frame
  4. The wooden ledge
  5. The yellow knit blanket
  6. The sleeping tabby kitten
Why this techniquePaint along, back to front
ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

Paint-along, back to front, is the beginner method and the only technique with version 2 keys: wall and window first, then the wooden sill, the blanket, the cat's body, its stripes and white fur, and the face details last.

Passed onBlock in, then build up (acrylic-block-in-beginner.yaml)

It has no version 2 keys (v2_step_range, v2_rules), so pipeline v3 can't plan with it; the owner also made paint-along the beginner default.

How the paint recipes were worked out16 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

Why the steps go in this order20 steps

Back to front: sky, wall and garden first, then the window frame and the ledge so the room is done; then the blanket, dark loops before light; then the kitten as a flat shape, shaded, given white patches, ears and nose, stripes and fur, with the sleeping face and whiskers last, where the eye lands.

  1. 1. Blend the sky through the window

    The farthest thing, the sky through the window, goes on first while the canvas is bare.

  2. 2. Blend the blue wall

    The wall is the other far thing; it runs under everything that sits in front of it.

  3. 3. Dab the dark leaves outside

    The trees outside go over the dry sky, dark first so the light taps can sit on top.

  4. 4. Dab the sunlit leaves

    Sunlit tops on the leaf clumps, once the dark taps are down.

  5. 5. Block in the white window frame

    The frame sits in front of the garden and the wall, so it goes on after both.

  6. 6. Shade the side of the frame

    Shadowed faces make the flat frame solid; they need the white under them dry.

  7. 7. Lay in the wooden ledge

    The ledge fills the bottom band, under where the blanket will lie.

  8. 8. Darken the front of the ledge

    Shadow on the ledge away from the window, before the light patches.

  9. 9. Dry-brush the sunlit patches on the ledge

    Sunlit patches last on the ledge, dry-brushed over the dry brown; the room is then done.

  10. 10. Block in the yellow blanket

    The blanket sits on the finished ledge, as one flat shape first.

  11. 11. Press in the dark knit loops

    Dark knit loops and the grooves give the blanket its form.

  12. 12. Press in the light knit loops

    Light loops on the tops of the rolls, over the dark ones.

  13. 13. Block in the kitten

    The kitten lies on the finished blanket, so it goes on as one flat gray shape now.

  14. 14. Shade the kitten's underside

    Dark gray turns the flat shape round before any markings go on.

  15. 15. Paint the white muzzle, chest and paws

    The white muzzle, paws and chest go on the shaded body before the stripes.

  16. 16. Paint the pink ears and nose

    Small color accents on the head before the stripes cross it.

  17. 17. Pull the tabby stripes

    The stripes follow the body's curve, now that the form and white patches are set.

  18. 18. Flick in the light fur

    Fur flicks soften the coat over the stripes.

  19. 19. Line the closed eyes and mouth

    The sleeping face is the focal point and goes on near the end, on dry paint.

  20. 20. Pull the white whiskers

    Thin white whiskers are the very last marks, over everything around the face.

Where Claude drew diagrams5 steps, free

Five steps build a shape or place lines by structure and got a diagram: the window frame, the blanket, the kitten, its stripes and its face. The rest are blends, dabs, fills and repeated marks that the picture and words carry. Step 18's picture shows small dark touches where the words ask for pale flicks; that is left and on the page under Known problems.

  • Step 5: Block in the white window frame beginner check

    Noticed: A frame of several pieces appears whole in one step, and where the post, crossbar and sill join isn't obvious from the picture.

    Pieces: The tall post first, then a crossbar near the top, then a wide sill slanting down to the left, in the order the words give.

  • Step 10: Block in the yellow blanket beginner check

    Noticed: The folded blanket appears whole in one flat shape; a beginner would not know it is an oval top over a rolled front.

    Pieces: A long low oval for the top, a rounded band in front of it, then both ends rounded, as the words say.

  • Step 13: Block in the kitten beginner check

    Noticed: A whole curled animal appears in one step; it is the hardest drawing in the lesson.

    Pieces: A big body oval, a head circle overlapping its left end, two triangle ears, then the tail and front legs as one curved piece along the front, as the words build it.

  • Step 17: Pull the tabby stripes beginner check

    Noticed: The stripes' placement depends on the body's curve, which a beginner would paint as straight bars.

    Pieces: The block-in shapes as done, then short forehead stripes, long curves over the back, and bands across the tail.

  • Step 19: Line the closed eyes and mouth beginner check

    Noticed: A face's features: where the closed eyes and mouth sit on a tilted head isn't clear from a 384-px picture.

    Pieces: The head, muzzle and nose as done, then the lower eye, the upper eye toward the top ear, and the small mouth above the paws.

A second Claude, with fresh eyes and none of this reasoning, compared each picture with its neighbors and the finish. It gets two rounds of fixes, then stops; anything still off is flagged on its step. A third checked each step's words against a measured map of what the picture changed, asking whether a beginner following them would get there.

Re-rendered once from the first finish and the photo with that fix; the second finish's wall measures #9bb1cc and the rest is unchanged (first finish kept as trials/99_finish_first.png).

What Claude would do differentlyfor the next lesson
  • The finish prompt's limited palette (ultramarine named) pushed a muted grey-blue wall to saturated cobalt on the first try; naming the wall's muted mix in the redo fixed it.
  • Helpers: the steps 0-1 helper was given the photo and steps 0 and 1 (setup, canvas fit, reference, finish); the plan writer was given v3/plan-brief.md with the photo, the reference and the finish, and picked its library files (picks.json, library/); the chain checker was given v3/chain-check.md and the folder chain/looks; the lesson's writer was given words/lesson (brief.md, then feedback.md twice, arc-brief.md and arc-feedback.md); the finisher (me) was given review.json's inputs, step E and steps/8-finish.md 8a to 8c's seal.
  • Two paints were fitted far from their plan colors (Leaf green to a blue-gray, Light gray to a mid-dark gray); the second shows as step 18's picture laying dark touches while its words ask for pale flicks. A plan naming the flicks' lightness more strongly might steer the chain; it would need a new chain, so it was left.
  • Several stroke cards (x-stroke, build-from-pieces, horizontal-strokes, curved-strokes, thick-to-thin, flicking) have no load or mistakes lines, so many steps have no load or watch-out line.
